title: Physical Assessment in Musculoskeletal Problems
path: Management of Clients with Musculoskeletal Problems

headings.title: Introduction to Musculoskeletal Physical Assessment
headings.content: Physical assessment of the musculoskeletal system is a fundamental competency for nursing students practicing in Nigeria. It allows nurses to identify structural abnormalities, evaluate functional status, and monitor changes in a patient's condition over time. Musculoskeletal assessments involve a systematic examination of bones, joints, muscles, and surrounding soft tissues. By integrating history-taking with objective physical techniques—namely inspection, palpation, and range of motion testing—nurses can differentiate between normal variations and pathological conditions such as fractures, arthritis, or muscle wasting. In the Nigerian healthcare context, where community health outreach and acute hospital care often intersect, mastering these skills enables early detection of debilitating conditions. Furthermore, a thorough baseline musculoskeletal assessment ensures that subsequent nursing interventions are tailored to promote mobility, prevent secondary complications such as contractures or pressure ulcers, and facilitate timely referrals to physicians or physiotherapists. Understanding the anatomical and physiological principles underlying these assessments prepares students for clinical placements and licensing examinations.

headings.title: Preparation, Environment, and Patient Positioning
headings.content: Proper preparation, environment, and patient positioning are critical for an accurate and comfortable musculoskeletal physical assessment. The nursing student must ensure that the examination room is well-lit to clearly observe skin color, contour changes, and subtle joint swellings. Privacy is paramount; adequate screening or a private room must be provided, especially since the patient may need to undress or wear a hospital gown to expose the joints being examined. The ambient temperature should be comfortable to prevent shivering, which can cause muscle tension and interfere with accurate muscle tone evaluation. Before touching the patient, the nurse should explain the procedure clearly, gain informed consent, and ensure proper hand hygiene. Patient positioning depends entirely on the specific body part being assessed. Generally, the patient should be placed in a comfortable, upright sitting position for inspecting the spine and upper extremities, and a supine position for examining the lower extremities and performing passive range of motion. Ensuring the examination bed is at a safe, ergonomic working height also protects the nurse from strain during palpation and manipulation.

headings.title: Inspection of Posture, Gait, and Alignment
headings.content: Inspection of posture, gait, and alignment provides immediate clues about a patient's musculoskeletal health. The nurse begins by observing the patient's posture while standing and sitting, looking for normal spinal curvatures such as cervical, thoracic, and lumbar curves, and noting any abnormal curvatures like kyphosis, lordosis, or scoliosis. Symmetry is a key principle; the nurse compares bilateral body parts, noting any asymmetry in shoulder height, iliac crests, or limb length, which may indicate underlying skeletal deformities or compensatory mechanisms. Gait assessment involves watching the patient walk across the room, observing their balance, stride length, arm swing, and foot placement. A smooth, coordinated, and rhythmic gait signifies a healthy musculoskeletal and neurological system, whereas an antive, shuffling, or ataxic gait suggests pain, weakness, neurological deficits, or joint instability. In Nigerian clinical practice, observing how a patient ambulates into the consulting room often serves as an informal yet vital initial screening tool before formal documentation begins. The nurse must note any assistive devices used, such as walking sticks or crutches, and evaluate whether the patient bears weight equally on both limbs.

headings.title: Palpation of Bones, Joints, and Surrounding Soft Tissues
headings.content: Palpation is the next step in musculoskeletal assessment, allowing the nurse to gather tactile data about bones, joints, and surrounding soft tissues. The nurse should use gentle, systematic pressure, comparing bilateral structures to establish a baseline. When palpating bones and joints, the nurse assesses for tenderness, swelling, crepitus (a crunching or grating sound/sensation), warmth, and nodules. Increased local skin temperature over a joint often indicates inflammation, infection, or acute arthritis. Crepitus, when felt or heard during joint movement, suggests cartilage wear or bony irregularities, commonly seen in osteoarthritis. Surrounding soft tissues, including muscles, tendons, and ligaments, should be palpated for tone, consistency, and tenderness. Muscle spasms or trigger points can frequently be identified during this phase, causing localized pain that restricts movement. The nurse must communicate continuously with the patient during palpation to gauge pain intensity and localized discomfort, ensuring that excessive pressure is avoided on visibly traumatized or fractured areas to prevent further injury.

headings.title: Assessment of Range of Motion (Active and Passive)
headings.content: Assessment of range of motion (ROM) evaluates the mobility of joints and is divided into active and passive movements. Active range of motion occurs when the patient moves the joint independently through its full arc of movement, demonstrating both joint mobility and muscle strength. Passive range of motion occurs when the nurse or examiner gently moves the patient's relaxed joint through its full arc without the patient exerting force. Passive movement helps determine the true limit of joint mobility and helps isolate joint capsule or ligament restrictions from muscle weakness. During ROM assessment, the nurse looks for limitations, pain, or instability. If a limitation is discovered, the nurse should measure the degree of movement using a goniometer for precise clinical documentation. Common movements evaluated include flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, pronation, supination, internal rotation, and external rotation. The nurse must stop immediately if the patient experiences sharp pain or muscle spasm, ensuring patient safety and preventing structural damage to healing tissues or unstable joints.

headings.title: Muscle Strength Testing and Grading
headings.content: Muscle strength testing and grading provide objective data regarding neuromuscular function. The standard system for grading muscle strength ranges from 0 to 5. A grade of 5 indicates normal muscle strength, where the muscle can move through full range of motion against complete resistance. A grade of 4 represents good strength, with movement against moderate resistance. A grade of 3 denotes fair strength, where the muscle can move against gravity alone, but not against any added resistance. A grade of 2 indicates poor strength, meaning the muscle can achieve full range of motion only when gravity is eliminated, such as with passive-assisted horizontal sliding. A grade of 1 is trace strength, where a slight flicker of contraction is palpable or visible, but no actual joint movement occurs. A grade of 0 represents complete paralysis with zero muscle contraction. To perform this testing, the nurse instructs the patient to flex or extend specific joints while applying opposing manual resistance. Bilateral comparison is crucial because normal baseline strength varies among individuals based on age, sex, and physical conditioning.

headings.title: Neurovascular Assessment of the Extremities
headings.content: Neurovascular assessment of the extremities is an essential nursing duty, particularly for patients with fractures, casts, traction, or post-operative orthopedic procedures. The assessment follows the mnemonic '5 Ps': Pain, Pallor, Pulses, Paresthesia, and Paralysis (with sometimes 'Polar' or temperature added as a sixth). The nurse evaluates distal pulses (such as the dorsalis pedis for the lower extremities or radial pulse for the upper extremities) to ensure adequate arterial blood flow. Capillary refill time is measured by pressing the nail bed and observing the return of pink color, which should normally occur within two seconds. Skin temperature of the extremity is checked using the back of the hand; a cool or cold limb suggests impaired circulation. Sensation is assessed by asking the patient if they feel light touch, numbness, or tingling (paresthesia), which indicates nerve integrity or compression. Finally, motor function is tested by asking the patient to wiggle their fingers or toes. Prompt identification of neurovascular compromise is vital because untreated ischemia can lead to permanent nerve damage, compartment syndrome, or limb loss.

headings.title: Special Diagnostic Tests for Specific Musculoskeletal Conditions
headings.content: Special diagnostic tests are utilized during physical assessment to isolate specific musculoskeletal pathologies, ligaments, meniscus tears, or nerve impingements. For example, the Phalen's test and Tinel's sign are commonly performed to assess for carpal tunnel syndrome, where compression of the median nerve at the wrist causes numbness and tingling. In knee assessments, the McMurray test is used to evaluate for tears in the meniscus by flexing and rotating the knee while listening or feeling for a click. The Lachman test or anterior drawer test is employed to check the integrity of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) of the knee joint. For the spine and hip, the Straight Leg Raise test helps determine if a patient has lumbar nerve root irritation or a herniated disc, reproducing radiating pain down the leg when elevated. Nursing students must learn how to properly perform and interpret these maneuvers, understanding that while these tests provide strong clinical indicators, they are typically confirmed with advanced imaging such as X-rays, MRI, or arthroscopy.

headings.title: Documentation and Abnormal Findings in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Accurate documentation and the ability to recognize abnormal findings are crucial responsibilities in nursing practice. Documentation must be objective, descriptive, and concise, avoiding vague terms like 'normal' or 'good' when specific measurements and descriptors can be used. The nurse should record posture, gait abnormalities, joint swelling, tenderness location, exact active and passive range of motion degrees, muscle strength grades, and neurovascular status. Recognizing abnormal findings—such as joint crepitus, asymmetry, muscle atrophy, abnormal curvatures, absent pulses, or cool extremities—allows nurses to detect clinical deterioration early and communicate effectively with the interprofessional healthcare team. In Nigerian hospitals, maintaining thorough and legally sound nursing notes ensures continuity of care across different shifts and protects both the patient and the healthcare provider. Any sudden changes, especially in neurovascular status, must be reported immediately as emergency findings to prevent permanent disability.
